content:
You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

Explain the difference between the World Wide Web and the Internet.

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

name: read
content:
1	What is the Internet?
     2	The Internet began in 1969 as a project of the U.S. Department of Defense called ARPANET, or
     3	Advanced Research Projects Agency Network. The goal of this project was to design a
     4	nationwide computer network that could withstand major disasters. If one part of the network
     5	was destroyed, the other parts would continue to function due to the decentralized structure of
     6	the network.
     7	In the early days of ARPANET, there were four computers in the United States attached to the
     8	network. Today, there are millions all over the world. Most people define the Internet as a
     9	collection of computer networks, but what exactly is a network? A network is a group of two or
    10	more computers connected together with cables that allow the computers to share information.
    11	Computers that are “on the Internet” all use the same protocols to send information back and
    12	forth, allowing them to communicate with each other. As long as a computer uses these
    13	protocols, it doesn't matter what type of hardware or software it uses.
    14	In the Internet's early days (the 1960s and 1970s), only government, military, and educational
    15	institutions had computers connected to the Internet. The Internet was originally designed for
    16	research and scholarly communication. But as it grew, its services became more popular, and
    17	new ways of using the Internet multiplied. For example, the Internet began to be used for
    18	informal communication, entertainment, and eventually commerce, as more businesses
    19	connected to the Internet in the 1990s. According to statistics compiled by Nua Internet Surveys
    20	Ltd., some 605.60 million people worldwide were connected to the Internet as of September
    21	2002.
    22	Today, the Internet remains decentralized, but it is no longer structured entirely around
    23	government computers. It is comprised of independently owned and managed individual
    24	networks of all sizes. The larger networks with high-speed connections are sometimes called
    25	backbone providers.
    26	Internet Service Providers (ISPs) lease Internet connections from the backbone providers and
    27	sell connections (also called Internet accounts) to consumers. Most home and small business
    28	users connect to the Internet with dial-up accounts to ISPs using a modem and special
    29	communications software.
    30	Uses for the Internet
    31	The Internet has a special significance for the library community because it allows patrons --
    32	both children and adults -- who do not have computers to keep up with the Internet for business
    33	and academic purposes. Libraries, to a great extent, help bridge what is called the "digital
    34	divide." The services listed below would be unattainable for many unless they were provided
    35	free of charge by the community's public library.
    36	· E-mail allows libraries and patrons to send messages back and forth to individuals or
    37	groups.
    38	· Telnet allows libraries and patrons to connect to a remote computer and use it as if you
    39	were there.
    40	· File Transfer Protocol (FTP) allows libraries to transfer files to and from other
    41	computers.
    42	· Usenet allows libraries and patrons to participate in group discussions on specific topics.
    43	· Internet Relay Chat (IRC) allows libraries and patrons to chat in real time with one or
    44	many users.
    45	· World Wide Web allows libraries and patrons access to literally millions of Web sites
    46	worldwide.
    47	What is the World Wide Web?
    48	One reason for the Internet's growth explosion is the ease of use and popularity of the World
    49	Wide Web and its graphical, “point-and-click” user interface. The World Wide Web was invented
    50	in 1989 by Tim Berners-Lee, a scientist at the European Particle Physics Laboratory (CERN) in
    51	Geneva, Switzerland. Lee wanted to make the information he used for research on the Internet
    52	more organized and accessible.
    53	The World Wide Web is based on hypertext, which is a method of linking documents using
    54	embedded hyperlinks. Hyperlinks can be text, which is usually underlined or a different color
    55	than the main text, or graphics. World Wide Web documents are created using a special
    56	computer language called HTML (Hypertext Markup Language). HTML coding embeds clickable
    57	links in documents and enables simple formatting.
    58	Documents written in HTML are stored in computers called servers. Any Internet user who has
    59	a Web browser can retrieve the documents. A Web browser is a computer program that knows
    60	how to read and display hypertext documents. It also knows how to communicate with servers
    61	that store HTML files. The protocol used for this kind of communication is called Hypertext
    62	Transfer Protocol (HTTP). Documents on the World Wide Web are called Web pages. Web
    63	pages are organized into Web sites. Each Web page has its own address, known formally as a
    64	Uniform Resource Locator or URL.
    65	Here is a made-up example of a URL for a page on the CNN site:
    66	http://www.cnn.com/WEATHER/cities/asiapcf.html.
    67	· http:// is the protocol used to retrieve the document.
    68	· www.cnn.com is the domain name for the server where the document is stored.
    69	· /WEATHER/cities/ is the path to the document in the server's directory structure.
    70	· asiapcf.html is the name of the actual HTML file.
    71	When you enter a URL in a Web browser, or if you click a hypertext link, the browser sends a
    72	message using the HTTP protocol to the computer identified in the URL. This message contains
    73	a request for the document specified in the URL. The server sends a copy of the document back
    74	to the browser, and it is displayed on your screen.
    75	Understanding a few things about URLs and other Internet addresses can make using the Web
    76	a lot easier. The domain name (the name of the computer) in a URL can be assigned by a large
    77	number of businesses. Just type "domain name" into your search engine, and you will find
    78	companies who can register your top level domain name. The Internet Corporation for Assigned
    79	Names and Numbers (ICANN) Web site at www.icann.org has a long list of accredited domain
    80	name registrars. There are standard suffixes for domain names, called extensions, which help
    81	identify what type of organization owns the domain. For example, domain names ending in .com
    82	indicate a commercial organization.
    83	Common extensions to domain names include:
    84	· .net is used for major networks (such as a backbone provider), but is also in general use
    85	· .edu is used for colleges and universities.
    86	· .gov is used for U.S. federal government agencies.
    87	· .mil is used for U.S. military organizations.
    88	· .org is commonly used for nonprofit and other organizations.
    89	Because so many domain names were snapped up at a rapid pace, more top level domains
    90	have been created. In the latter part of 2000, ICANN selected seven new top-level domains
    91	(TLDs):
    92	· .aero is used to the air transport industry.
    93	· .biz is used for all-purpose business sites.
    94	· .coop is used for cooperatives.
    95	· .info has unrestricted use.
    96	· .museum is used for museums.
    97	· .name is used for individual Web sites.
    98	· .pro is used for professionals such as doctors, lawyers, accountants, and others.
    99	Domain names in countries outside the United States usually end with a two-letter code
   100	representing the country; for example, Canadian Web sites end in .ca. Some state and county
   101	Web pages, including many belonging to libraries, have domain names ending in .us.

(doc.txt) It also notes that "Computers that are 'on the Internet' all use the same protocols to send information back and forth, allowing them to communicate with each other." (doc.txt) The Internet began in 1969 as ARPANET, "a project of the U.S. Department of Defense," originally designed so that "If one part of the network was destroyed, the other parts would continue to function due to the decentralized structure of the network." (doc.txt)

**The World Wide Web** is a document-based system that runs on top of that infrastructure. The document states: "The World Wide Web was invented in 1989 by Tim Berners-Lee, a scientist at the European Particle Physics Laboratory (CERN) in Geneva, Switzerland." (doc.txt) It is "based on hypertext, which is a method of linking documents using embedded hyperlinks." (doc.txt) Its documents are written in HTML, stored on servers, and "Documents on the World Wide Web are called Web pages. Web pages are organized into Web sites." (doc.txt) A user retrieves them with "a Web browser," a "computer program that knows how to read and display hypertext documents," using "the protocol... called Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP)." (doc.txt)

**How they relate:** The document lists the World Wide Web as one of the "Uses for the Internet," alongside e-mail, Telnet, FTP, Usenet, and IRC: "World Wide Web allows libraries and patrons access to literally millions of Web sites worldwide." (doc.txt) It also says "Any Internet user who has a Web browser can retrieve the documents." (doc.txt) And it credits the Web with driving the Internet's popularity: "One reason for the Internet's growth explosion is the ease of use and popularity of the World Wide Web and its graphical, 'point-and-click' user interface." (doc.txt)

So, in the document's terms: the Internet is the collection of interconnected computer networks (the plumbing), while the World Wide Web is a hypertext system of linked HTML documents and Web sites that is one of the services available over the Internet. The document does not contain a single explicit sentence defining the Web as a subset of the Internet; the relationship is shown by listing the Web among the Internet's uses and by noting that Internet users retrieve Web documents.
